paper.title: Cross-Embodiment Offline Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Robot Datasets

read: full text: Sections 1-7 and Appendices B-C (datasets, rewards), D (architecture, skimmed), E (robot graphs, FGW, group assignments), F (gradient-conflict histograms), G (TD3+BC repeat), H (grouping the critic), I (hyperparameters, skimmed)

claims.claim: Pretraining one locomotion policy on pooled data from many different robot bodies with offline reinforcement learning, rather than behaviour cloning, pays off when much of the pooled data is suboptimal, and the pooled pretraining speeds up learning on a robot left out of it. Supported only if, averaged over the pooled datasets that are mostly suboptimal, the offline-RL policy earns higher return than behaviour cloning with the same network, while the two are within noise on expert-only data; and if, for every held-out robot tested, starting from the pooled pretrained network reaches a good policy in fewer updates than training that robot from scratch.
claims.decision_rule: Mean return over suboptimal-rich pooled datasets: offline RL > BC; ~equal on expert data; leave-one-out pretraining converges faster for every held-out robot.

claims.claim: When one offline-RL policy is trained on pooled data from many robot bodies, the robots that end up worse off than if trained alone are hurt because their policy-gradient updates conflict with those of morphologically dissimilar robots, and these conflicts grow with the share of suboptimal data and with how varied the bodies are. Supported only if the fraction of robot pairs whose per-robot actor gradients point in opposing directions rises both as the suboptimal share of the data increases and as more, and more varied, robots are pooled; if, among robots whose return changes substantially under pooling, the change correlates positively and strongly with how aligned that robot's gradients are with the others'; if a measure of morphological similarity between robot pairs correlates significantly with their gradient alignment; and if these relationships also hold under a second offline-RL algorithm.
claims.decision_rule: Negative-cosine fraction rises with suboptimal share and with embodiment diversity; transfer gain vs mean gradient cosine strongly positive; morphology similarity vs gradient cosine significant; replicated with a second algorithm.

claims.claim: In offline reinforcement learning on pooled multi-robot data, updating the policy separately for fixed groups of robots chosen by morphological similarity makes the pooled policy better than updating on all robots at once and better than existing generic methods for resolving gradient conflicts between tasks, with the largest gains when most data are suboptimal. Supported only if it gives the highest mean return across all the expert, replay and mostly-suboptimal datasets; if on the mostly-suboptimal datasets it improves on plain pooled training by at least 20%; if grouping by morphology beats both random grouping and a coarse grouping by body type; and if its advantage survives giving the baseline the same number of optimiser steps and processed samples.
claims.decision_rule: Best mean return over six datasets vs IQL, PCGrad, selective grouping; >=20% over IQL on 70%-suboptimal sets; beats random and body-type grouping; holds under compute normalization.

experiments.text: Build a pooled multi-robot locomotion benchmark with controlled data quality. Setup: 16 simulated robots in MuJoCo (nine quadrupeds, six bipeds, one hexapod), each trained with PPO to walk at a commanded 1 m/s forward or backward under a shared dense reward with robot-specific weights. For each robot and direction build three 1M-step datasets: expert rollouts of the converged policy, the whole training replay up to expert level (about 500M steps) subsampled uniformly, and a mix of 700k early, suboptimal steps with 300k late steps. A single network takes a shared observation part plus variable-length joint and foot sets aggregated by attention conditioned on morphology descriptors, extended with an action encoder for a Q-function. Each method uses about 100M sampled transitions per robot; report final return, mean +/- standard error over 5 seeds.

Compare offline RL with behaviour cloning on pooled data. Setup: implicit Q-learning and behaviour cloning with the same architecture, trained on all 16 robots for each of the six datasets. Result: on expert data they tie (63.39 vs 63.31 forward, 67.10 vs 67.17 backward); on replay data offline RL wins (54.61 vs 49.71, 51.86 vs 42.87); on the mostly-suboptimal data it wins forward (36.62 vs 30.52) but loses backward (38.69 vs 41.42). Means are 52.05 against 49.17.

Test whether pooled pretraining helps a robot it did not include. Setup: leave-one-out: pretrain with offline RL on the pooled data minus one robot, then fine-tune on that robot, against training on that robot from scratch; plot evaluation return against update steps for a quadruped (Badger) and two bipeds (Unitree G1, Cassie). Result: the pretrained network converges markedly faster for all three.

Establish where pooling helps and where it hurts. Setup: for each robot compare implicit Q-learning trained on that robot alone against the pooled 16-robot model, on expert forward data and on mostly-suboptimal forward data. Result: on expert data pooling changes nothing (means 63.30 vs 63.35). On suboptimal data some quadrupeds gain a lot (Unitree A1 14.55 to 27.38, Go1 14.46 to 40.05, Go2 13.76 to 52.39, Badger 15.98 to 40.53) while bipeds with few similar bodies in the pool collapse (Unitree H1 54.47 to 6.00, G1 78.93 to 0.86); the mean drops from 39.42 to 37.57.

Measure gradient conflict between robots and relate it to transfer. Setup: compute each robot's actor gradient from the advantage-weighted regression loss during training and the pairwise cosine similarity between robots; report the fraction of negative pairs for expert, 30%-suboptimal and 70%-suboptimal data, and for growing robot sets (three similar Unitree quadrupeds, all nine quadrupeds, all 16 robots); correlate, for robots whose return changes by more than 10 under pooling, the change with that robot's mean cosine to the others. Result: the negative fraction rises from 0.159 to 0.268 to 0.323 with suboptimal share and from 0.153 to 0.288 to 0.323 with diversity, with the negative mass shifting toward -1; the transfer-gain correlation is r = 0.815.

Check that morphological distance predicts which robots conflict. Setup: represent each robot as a graph of torso, joints and feet with node features for relative position and control parameters; compute pairwise Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distances, normalise to [0,1] and convert to similarity; correlate with mean pairwise gradient cosine across all robot pairs. Result: quadrupeds cluster together in both matrices, and similarity correlates with gradient alignment at Pearson r = 0.63 (p = 1.3e-14).

Rule out that the conflict pattern is specific to one algorithm's actor update. Setup: repeat the per-robot pooled-versus-alone comparison and all gradient-conflict analyses with TD3+BC. Result: pooling again devastates several bipeds (H1 33.44 to 1.42, G1 66.71 to 1.94, Talos 73.97 to 6.14), the negative-cosine fraction again rises with suboptimal share and diversity, transfer change correlates with gradient alignment at r = 0.766, and morphological similarity with alignment at r = 0.711 (p = 8.9e-20).

Compare morphology-grouped updates against plain pooling and generic conflict-resolution methods. Setup: cluster robots hierarchically on the morphological distance matrix into fixed groups, do one shared critic update per iteration and then one actor update per group in shuffled order; compare behaviour cloning, TD3+BC and implicit Q-learning, implicit Q-learning with gradient projection (PCGrad) and with dynamic affinity-based task grouping, and grouped versions of all three base learners, on all six datasets. Result: grouped implicit Q-learning has the highest mean (57.29 vs 52.05 plain, 55.07 affinity grouping, 53.48 PCGrad) and on the mostly-suboptimal data reaches 51.19 and 49.60 against 36.62 and 38.69; its average gain over plain pooling there is 33.99% against 18.33% and 7.15% for the two conflict-resolution methods. Grouping also lifts behaviour cloning by 26.3% and TD3+BC by 19.5% on those splits. It is not best everywhere: on expert-replay forward data grouped TD3+BC (57.04) and plain TD3+BC (55.66) beat it (54.62).

Rule out that any partition of the robots would help. Setup: on 70%-suboptimal forward data compare plain pooled implicit Q-learning, random grouping, a coarse four-way split by body type (bipeds, quadrupeds, hexapods, torso-less bipeds) and morphology-distance grouping. Result: 37.57 for plain pooling, 38.73 (+3.1%) for random groups, 34.45 (-8.3%) for the body-type split and 51.98 (+38.3%) for morphology-distance groups.

Rule out that the gain comes from taking more optimiser steps. Grouping performs one actor update per group per iteration, so the baseline gets fewer updates. Setup: give plain pooled implicit Q-learning M times as many optimiser steps with batches 1/M as large, so steps and processed samples both match, and compare on 70%-suboptimal forward data; separately sweep the number of groups M over {1, 2, 4, 7, 10, 13}. Result: the normalised baseline reaches 44.20 +/- 2.22 against 51.98 +/- 1.70 for grouping; performance peaks at moderate M (best at 7, with 2-4 already strong) and declines slightly with excessive partitioning, while wall-clock time grows with M.

dropped: Applying grouping to the critic as well (no gain; 3 seeds); dataset reward-distribution descriptions.
notes: c0 bar uses the mean over suboptimal-rich datasets because BC beats IQL on 70%-suboptimal backward (41.42 vs 38.69).
